title: Technical SEO Tips for Moving Companies
html:
A moving company's quote form loading blank on a customer's phone during peak season costs real bookings. So does a service area page buried so deep in your site that Google never crawls it. These technical SEO tips for moving companies focus on the specific structural failures that kill local search visibility before a single customer sees your trucks. Moving company websites face technical SEO challenges that most local businesses don't. Quote forms must load fast on mobile because customers search mid-move, under stress, and on phones -- not desktops. Service area pages covering multiple cities are often buried in subfolders with no internal links pointing to them, so Google ignores them. MovingCompany schema requires DOT numbers and FMCSA registration data that generic LocalBusiness schema doesn't include. Fixing these three areas -- page speed on quote-critical pages, crawl access to city pages, and mover-specific structured data -- directly improves local pack rankings and form submission rates.

1. Fix Page Speed on Your Quote Form Pages

Why it matters: Google's Core Web Vitals data shows that pages with an LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) above 3.5 seconds lose a significant share of mobile form submissions before the page fully loads. Moving customers aren't browsing -- they have a move date and they're getting quotes from three companies at once. The slowest site loses. Page speed is one of the core pillars of home service technical SEO that directly affects how Google ranks your quote pages in local search. Fixing it is one of the highest-ROI moves in any SEO strategy for movers.

  • Run your quote page URL specifically through PageSpeed Insights, not just your homepage.
  • Convert truck and crew photos to WebP format. A raw JPEG from a smartphone can run 4--6MB. The WebP version of the same image should be under 200KB.
  • Defer non-critical JavaScript so the quote form loads before page tracking scripts fire.
  • Use a CDN if you cover multiple service areas. A customer in a market two states away shouldn't wait for assets to load from your home server.

Running PageSpeed on the homepage, seeing a passing score, and assuming the quote page is fine. Quote pages often load heavier due to embedded forms, chat widgets, and tracking pixels that don't appear on the homepage.

2. Add MovingCompany Schema With DOT and FMCSA Data

Why it matters: Generic LocalBusiness schema doesn't tell Google you're a licensed carrier. MovingCompany schema lets you include your DOT number, FMCSA registration, and operating authority -- signals that separate licensed movers from unlicensed competitors in the same market.

  • Use MovingCompany schema type on your homepage and primary service pages.
  • Include your DOT number in the taxID or identifier field.
  • Add your operating authority states in the areaServed field -- specific state codes, not just city names.
  • Validate using Google's Rich Results Test before publishing. Check that your business name, phone number, and service areas match exactly what appears on your Google Business Profile.

Copying schema from another moving company's site without updating the DOT number, phone number, or service area fields. Mismatched data between your schema and your GBP creates a trust conflict that suppresses local pack visibility.

3. Make Mobile the Priority on Every Quote Touch Point

Why it matters: Moving is a high-stress, time-sensitive decision. Most customers search on a phone while standing in their current home trying to figure out logistics. A quote form that requires pinching, zooming, or three scrolls to find the "Submit" button loses the job to a competitor whose form works in two taps.

  • Test your quote form on a real phone, not just Chrome's mobile emulator.
  • Make the "Get a Quote" and "Call Now" buttons large enough to tap without zooming -- minimum 48x48 pixels per Google's tap target guidelines.
  • Show your full service area list and pricing details on mobile, not just on desktop. Hiding this information on smaller screens makes customers distrust the site.

Building a desktop quote form first and assuming responsive design handles the mobile version. Responsive frameworks adjust layout, but they don't fix forms with too many required fields, small input boxes, or dropdowns that don't work with a mobile keyboard.

4. Add Verifiable Trust Signals for E-E-A-T

Why it matters: Google's quality raters evaluate moving company sites for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trust. For movers specifically, the bar is high -- customers hand over their home address, their move date, and sometimes a deposit before the truck arrives. A site without verifiable identity signals ranks lower and converts worse.

Using anonymous content authors on moving guides. A blog post about "How to Pack a Kitchen for a Long-Distance Move" written by "Staff Writer" carries no E-E-A-T value. Name a real person on your team and add a two-sentence bio.

5. Fix the Architecture Around Your City Service Pages

Why it matters: Moving companies typically build city-specific pages like /locations/chicago-il/ or /service-areas/denver/ -- then never link to them from the homepage, the main service page, or any blog post. Google crawls what it can find through links. Pages with no internal links pointing to them often don't get crawled at all.

  • Run a site crawl using Screaming Frog or a similar tool. Export the list of pages with zero internal links pointing to them -- these are your orphaned city pages.
  • Link directly from your main navigation or a "Service Areas" hub page to every active city page.
  • Add internal links from your highest-traffic blog posts to the city page that matches the topic. A post about moving costs in Dallas should link to your Dallas service page.
  • Keep all city pages accessible within two clicks from the homepage.

Burying city pages inside subfolders with no parent page linking to them. A structure like /locations/midwest/illinois/chicago/ with no links from the homepage means Google may never crawl that page, even if you've submitted it in your sitemap.

6. Audit Crawl Efficiency for Multi-Market Sites

Why it matters: Moving companies that serve multiple metros often have hundreds of city pages, blog posts, and duplicate content variants. Google allocates a crawl budget to each site. If that budget gets spent on low-value pages -- thin duplicates, parameter URLs, or outdated service area pages -- your important pages get crawled less often.

  • Check Google Search Console's Coverage report. Look for pages marked "Crawled but not indexed" -- these are wasting crawl budget without producing search visibility.
  • Add canonical tags to any duplicate city pages that target the same market under different URLs.
  • Block low-value parameter URLs (like filtered search results or session IDs) using your robots.txt file.
  • Remove or consolidate city pages for markets you no longer serve. An active page for a city you stopped servicing two years ago drains budget and confuses searchers.

Submitting every page variant in the sitemap to force crawling. Google ignores sitemaps when it detects thin or duplicate content. Fix the content first, then resubmit.

Related Blog Posts

What is technical SEO for moving companies?

It's the process of fixing backend website issues that prevent Google from crawling, indexing, and ranking your pages in local search. For movers, this includes quote form speed, city page architecture, and MovingCompany schema with DOT data.

Why does page speed matter specifically for moving company websites?

Moving customers request multiple quotes in a short window. A quote page that takes more than 3 seconds to load on mobile loses form submissions to faster competitors before the page finishes loading.

What schema markup should moving companies use?

Use MovingCompany schema type, not just LocalBusiness. Include your DOT number, FMCSA registration, operating authority states, and service areas. Validate in Google's Rich Results Test before publishing.

Does mobile responsiveness affect local search rankings?

Yes. Google indexes the mobile version of your site first. A quote form that doesn't work properly on a phone directly affects both rankings and conversion rate.
